A 37-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She
states that it started 1 day ago and has not improved with hygiene products. She is sexually active and
uses condoms. She does not complain of any abdominal or pelvic pain but states she has some mild
burning when urinating. Her temperature is 99.2°F (36.4°C), blood pressure is 104/72 mmHg, pulse is
96/min, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable
for thick, white discharge from the cervix. There is no cervical motion or adnexal tenderness or masses.
Some whitish discharge is noted from the urethra. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the
following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Metronidazole and
clindamycin (B) Ceftriaxone and doxycycline (C) Ceftriaxone alone (D) Azithromycin alone (E)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (F) Metronidazole (G) Fluconazole (H) Amoxicillin-clavulanate (I)
Ceftriaxone and azithromycin (J) Clindamycin cream
 A. Metronidazole and clindamycin
B. Ceftriaxone and doxycycline
C. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin
D. Fluconazole
E. Azithromycin alone
F. Metronidazole
G. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
H. Ceftriaxone alone
I. Clindamycin cream

J. Amoxicillin-clavulanate
